pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: The paper’s observation that rapid cooling yields an amorphous structure and that reheating leads to primary crystallization, implying that surface-induced nucleation may be a critical pathway for crystallization.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces an external surface passivation intervention (oxide coating) not addressed in the paper, targeting the suppression of heterogeneous nucleation during reheating to enhance amorphous retention and thermal stability.

fields.hypothesis: Applying a thin, inert surface oxide coating (such as Al2O3) immediately after rapid quenching will suppress heterogeneous nucleation during subsequent reheating and thereby increase amorphous retention and thermal stability.
fields.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy produced by rapid cooling (melt-spun ribbon) exhibiting an amorphous structure with a tendency for primary crystallization on reheating.
fields.intervention: Deposit a nanometer-scale Al2O3 coating on the freshly produced amorphous alloy surface using techniques such as atomic layer deposition (ALD).
fields.conditions: The coating should be applied immediately after melt-spinning and before any reheating cycle; subsequent thermal analysis (DSC/thermography) should be performed in the reheating regime below 1370 K, with cooling rates comparable to those studied (10⁵–10⁶ K/s for quenching and reheating rates around 20 K/min).
fields.structural_mediator: The continuous oxide layer formed on the surface.
fields.mechanism: The Al2O3 coating acts as a diffusion barrier and physically passivates the surface, reducing atomic mobility and hindering the heterogeneous nucleation of crystalline phases during reheating. This reduces the formation of primary non‐eutectic crystalline phases and maintains the amorphous structure at higher temperatures.
fields.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy will exhibit a higher onset temperature for crystallization, a reduced exothermic peak related to primary crystallization in DSC curves, and improved thermal stability (up to a modestly higher thermal resistance margin, on the order of tens of Kelvin) relative to uncoated samples.
fields.baseline: Uncoated Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy, which shows extensive primary crystallization during slower cooling and reheating cycles as detailed in the paper.
fields.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective while the reheating temperature does not exceed the point where the coating itself degrades (likely below 1370 K) and in systems with similar cooling rates (10⁵–10⁶ K/s quenching).
fields.uncertainty: Precise quantitative improvements in thermal stability are uncertain; the degree of improvement depends on coating thickness uniformity and its adherence to the alloy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of melt-spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy ribbons. One set is subjected to an immediate ALD deposition of a thin (e.g., 10–20 nm) Al2O3 coating, while the control set remains uncoated. Both sets are then subjected to identical reheating cycles and DSC analysis.
measurements: DSC endothermic/exothermic peak temperatures and energies
XRD/TEM characterization after reheating to assess crystallinity
Surface characterization (SEM/EDS) to verify coating integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples show no statistically significant delay in the onset of crystallization (i.e., similar DSC exothermic peaks) or exhibit similar crystallinity on reheating as the control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: The intervention extends the general principle that heterogeneous nucleation at surfaces can drive crystallization, and applies a surface engineering solution—common in other casting applications—to a complex multi‐component metallic glass system.
pool.what_is_new: This approach introduces a novel, single processing intervention via mold surface modification to address crystallization issues in Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni–P alloys, an angle that has not been previously exploited in reported studies on similar systems.

fields.hypothesis: Employing a mold or substrate with a specifically engineered, chemically inert surface coating (e.g., a BN or Al2O3 layer) during casting will reduce heterogeneous nucleation at the mold-alloy interface, thereby increasing the amorphous phase retention and thermal stability of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
fields.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy cast in conventional metallic molds that tend to promote heterogeneous nucleation leading to extensive primary crystallization.
fields.intervention: Replace or coat the inner surface of the casting mold with a thin, high-melting, chemically inert barrier (such as boron nitride [BN] or alumina [Al2O3]) to minimize contact-induced heterogeneous nucleation during solidification.
fields.conditions: Casting should be performed under identical rapid cooling conditions (e.g., in melt spinning or copper mold casting) with a comparison between standard mold surfaces and those with the inert coating; reheating thermal analysis should be conducted over the typical range where crystallization exotherms are observed.
fields.structural_mediator: Reduced nucleation sites at the mold-alloy interface and more uniform cooling.
fields.mechanism: The inert coating acts as a physical and chemical barrier that prevents the formation of potent heterogeneous nucleation sites at the interface between the mold and the liquid alloy. By suppressing nucleation at the boundaries, the overall driving force for primary crystal formation is reduced, enabling the retention of a larger volume fraction of the amorphous phase. This concept takes advantage of well-known principles in casting and solidification where surface treatments are used to control nucleation (see TXT::wikipedia::Eutectic_system::008).
fields.predicted_outcome: The use of an inert-coated mold is predicted to lead to DSC curves with reduced or delayed crystallization exotherms, an increased onset temperature of crystallization, and XRD patterns indicating a higher amorphous content. The effect should be observable at cooling rates in the lower end of the achievable range (≈10^2 K∙s−1) where interface nucleation is more critical.
fields.baseline: Casting using conventional molds yields significant primary crystallization and a multistep crystallization sequence upon reheating.
fields.boundary: Casting should be performed at typical rapid cooling rates (e.g., 10^2–10^3 K∙s−1) and DSC reheating should traverse the glass transition and early crystallization intervals.
fields.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement depends on the quality and adherence of the coating; slight variabilities in coating uniformity may affect the reproducibility of the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Cast identical alloy samples in standard molds and in molds coated with BN or Al2O3. Use identical cooling conditions and then perform DSC analysis and XRD characterization on both sample sets to assess differences in crystallization behavior and amorphous content.
measurements: DSC crystallization onset temperature and exotherm intensity
XRD peak analysis for crystalline phase content
Optical or electron microscopy of microstructure near the mold-contact region
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant differences in the onset temperature, exotherm intensity, or amorphous phase fraction are observed between samples cast in coated and uncoated molds, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: the finding that high-entropy effects can be harnessed through controlled thermal treatments to induce a glass-to-glass transition that elevates the disorder and stabilizes the low-energy glass state (PMC9023469 series).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies the concept of inducing a high-entropy glass-to-glass transition—previously demonstrated in a NbNiZrTiCo metallic glass—to the more compositionally complex Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy, proposing an exact thermal intervention to overcome its tendency for primary crystallization.

fields.hypothesis: A controlled sub‐Tg annealing treatment immediately following melt‐spinning will induce a high-entropy glass-to-glass transition in the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy, thereby increasing its amorphous retention and thermal stability while suppressing primary crystallization.
fields.material_initial_state: Amorphous as-cast Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy produced via melt spinning, which displays multiple primary non-eutectic crystalline phases upon slower cooling and complex crystallization on reheating.
fields.intervention: Implement a heat treatment that rapidly reheats the as-cast amorphous alloy to a temperature just above its glass transition temperature (Tg) but below the onset of primary crystallization, and then cool it down, effectively triggering a glass-to-glass transition.
fields.conditions: Annealing temperature selected to lie in a narrow window (approximately Tg + 20–40 K) with a short dwell time (e.g., 1–2 minutes) followed by rapid cooling; melt-spinning cooling rates (≈10^6 K/s) for initial vitrification; reheating in a controlled DSC or furnace environment free from oxidation.
fields.structural_mediator: Short- and medium-range atomic rearrangements leading to increased ordering within the amorphous matrix without long-range crystallinity.
fields.mechanism: Inspired by the high-entropy effect observed in NbNiZrTiCo metallic glasses (PMC9023469::web::000 to ::024), the sub-Tg annealing allows controlled atomic rearrangement (a glass-to-glass transition) that reduces free volume and lowers the configurational energy. This altered atomic packing retards nucleation kinetics for primary crystallization, thereby enhancing thermal stability.
fields.predicted_outcome: A DSC scan of the treated alloy will show a suppressed or delayed exothermic crystallization peak and an increased onset temperature for crystallization, along with a distinct glass transition shift (e.g., a higher Tg or modified heat capacity step) relative to the untreated alloy.
fields.baseline: The untreated Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy displays extensive primary crystallization during slower cooling and multiple crystallization exotherms upon reheating.
fields.boundary: Effective if the annealing temperature is maintained safely below the onset of crystallization; too high a temperature or too long a dwell will lead to unavoidable crystallization.
fields.uncertainty: The precise temperature window and time necessary for optimum glass-to-glass transition in this specific alloy are not known a priori and will require calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbons via melt spinning and subject them to a series of sub-Tg annealing treatments at various temperatures and times. Compare the thermal behavior using DSC and structural state via XRD and TEM.
measurements: DSC scans to monitor the presence and shift of crystallization exotherms and glass transition signals
XRD to detect any onset of crystalline peaks
TEM for local structure analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sub-Tg annealing does not result in a measurable increase in the onset temperature of crystallization and fails to suppress the primary crystallization exotherm relative to untreated samples, or if it induces crystallinity, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C4
pool.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration that high local dislocation density and associated stress concentrations trigger crystalline-to-amorphous transformation in localized regions (e.g., crack tips).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes the use of a controlled, surface-confined mechanical attrition process (SMAT) to deliberately replicate the beneficial localized dislocation environment on the alloy’s surface, thereby promoting amorphization and thermal stability—a processing route distinct from previously considered bulk deformation methods.

fields.hypothesis: Tailored Surface Mechanical Attrition Treatment (SMAT) to Generate Nano-Structured, Dislocation-Rich Layers
fields.material_initial_state: Rapidly solidified Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy that, under conventional slow cooling and reheating, develops several primary crystalline phases with limited amorphous retention.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT) using small spherical media to impact the alloy surface, thereby inducing severe localized plastic deformation.
fields.conditions: Select SMAT parameters (impact energy, treatment duration, media size, and coverage) such that only a thin surface layer (e.g., sub-micron to a few microns thick) is affected. The treatment should be optimized to achieve ultra-high dislocation densities and grain refinement without causing macroscopic damage or excessive surface roughening.
fields.structural_mediator: A nanocrystalline, highly dislocated surface layer that mimics crack-tip conditions—featuring an intensive local dislocation network and lattice distortions acting as barriers to crystalline nucleation.
fields.mechanism: The rapid, localized impacts during SMAT generate extreme plastic deformation in the surface region, leading to dislocation tangles and grain refinement similar to the crack-tip environments discussed in the paper. This disordered, high-stress surface layer impedes the nucleation and propagation of primary crystalline phases during subsequent thermal processing, thereby increasing the retention of the amorphous phase and enhancing thermal stability.
fields.predicted_outcome: In contrast to untreated specimens, SMAT-treated samples will exhibit a surface layer with a significantly higher amorphous fraction and an upward shift in the crystallization onset temperature (potentially on the order of several tens of °C as determined by surface-sensitive thermal measurements), with TEM and XRD confirming the nanostructured, dislocation-rich character of the modified layer.
fields.baseline: The untreated alloy undergoes a complex multistep crystallization with predominant primary crystalline phase formation.
fields.boundary: The benefits are confined to the treated surface layer and depend on precise control of SMAT parameters; overly aggressive attrition could lead to excessive surface damage or unintended re-crystallization.
fields.uncertainty: While the mechanism is conceptually sound, the depth, uniformity, and bulk impact of the SMAT-induced amorphous layer are not fully predictable without experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set subjected to the tailored SMAT process and one untreated control. After identical slow cooling and reheating treatments, analyze the surface region using grazing-incidence DSC, XRD, and cross-sectional TEM to assess phase and microstructural differences.
measurements: Grazing-incidence DSC to detect shifts in the crystallization onset temperature of the surface layer
XRD (using grazing incidence) to quantify the fraction of the amorphous phase near the surface
TEM to image the nanocrystalline, dislocation-rich structure in the SMAT-treated layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SMAT-treated samples do not exhibit a significantly higher amorphous content and no clear, consistent increase in crystallization onset temperature (e.g., less than a 10 °C shift) compared to controls, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C5
pool.builds_on: The paper’s insight that glass formation is controlled by the competition between icosahedral and crystal-like order under moderate cooling conditions.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies a compositional modification (minor Boron addition) to tailor the atomic-scale structural fluctuations in a complex, multicomponent alloy, an intervention not reported or proposed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: A minor alloying addition of a glass‐forming element (e.g. ~2 at.% Boron) to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 will increase amorphous retention and enhance thermal stability by suppressing the growth of primary crystalline clusters.
fields.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy that undergoes extensive primary crystallization and multistep crystallization during solidification.
fields.intervention: Introduce a small (≈2 at.%) addition of Boron uniformly into the alloy composition.
fields.conditions: The alloy is processed under the same rapid cooling, moderate cooling, and subsequent reheating protocols as before, with cooling rates spanning from below 6.3×10^11 K/s to above 16.6×10^11 K/s, and reheating carried out in the temperature range that shows early crystallization onset (around 750–775 K).
fields.structural_mediator: Enhanced short-range icosahedral order and increased chemical disorder at the atomic level.
fields.mechanism: Boron is known to promote local icosahedral-like ordering and to increase the atomic packing frustration. This extra chemical heterogeneity raises the nucleation barrier for crystalline phases. In this way, the kinetic retardation of atomic rearrangement is enhanced, and the thermodynamic competition between icosahedral and crystal-like order is shifted toward the disordered (amorphous) state. This parallels the paper’s discussion of the competition between icosahedral and crystal-like clusters in the moderate cooling region (PMC4778031::web::009 and PMC4778031::web::014).
fields.predicted_outcome: The boron-doped alloy should exhibit a higher retained amorphous fraction during cooling and a delayed onset of crystallization upon reheating by thermal analysis, compared to the undoped alloy. The improvement is expected to be significant under conditions where the original alloy showed abnormal fluctuations in crystalline fraction.
fields.baseline: The original Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy’s behavior with extensive primary crystallization and fluctuating amorphous fractions in the moderate cooling rate regime.
fields.boundary: Improvement expected when cooling rates are in the critical fluctuation region (approximately 6.3×10^11–16.6×10^11 K/s) and reheating passes through 750–775 K; outside this temperature window, the effect may be less decisive.
fields.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improved thermal stability and the optimum boron content require experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: the baseline Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 and the same alloy with ~2 at.% Boron addition, processed under identical cooling and reheating protocols. Use differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and high-resolution TEM to monitor the onset of crystallization, amorphous fraction, and structural motifs.
measurements: DSC exothermic peak onset temperatures during reheating
Crystalline fraction determined via X-ray diffraction and TEM
Local atomic order assessed by electron diffraction or suitable spectroscopic methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Boron-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant delay in the onset of crystallization and does not retain a higher amorphous fraction (or if it shows adverse phase separation), then the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C6
pool.builds_on: the rapid-quenching mechanism for metallic glass formation as demonstrated by melt spinning in other alloy systems
pool.what_is_new: It specifies alloy-specific processing parameters (ribbon thickness, wheel speed) tailored to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 that have not been previously reported, directly addressing the unique crystallization kinetics of this high-entropy alloy.

fields.hypothesis: Tailor the melt spinning process for Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 by optimizing ribbon thickness and wheel speed to achieve an alloy‐specific critical cooling rate that kinetically suppresses nucleation of primary non‐eutectic phases.
fields.material_initial_state: Bulk-cast Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy showing multistep crystallization with extensive formation of primary crystalline phases under conventional cooling.
fields.intervention: Use melt spinning with a targeted ribbon thickness (<50 μm) and adjusted wheel speed to reliably reach cooling rates >10^6 K/s.
fields.conditions: During processing, ensure a cooling rate significantly above the estimated critical value (e.g., >10^6 K/s) and perform reheating using a controlled ramp that stays below the temperature onset of secondary crystallization.
fields.structural_mediator: The ultra-high cooling rate forces the melt into a deep undercooled state, drastically reducing atomic mobility and suppressing the nucleation and growth of crystalline phases.
fields.mechanism: By achieving cooling rates that exceed the alloy’s specific critical cooling rate (determined by its thermodynamic driving force and atomic size mismatch), the formation of ordered clusters necessary for primary crystallization is kinetically hindered. This traps the disordered (amorphous) arrangement, thereby improving thermal stability upon reheating.

fields.boundary: If the achieved cooling rate falls below the critical threshold (approximately <10^6 K/s), the intervention will not suppress nucleation effectively; furthermore, reheating rates must remain moderate to avoid triggering secondary crystallization.
fields.uncertainty: Exact values for the critical cooling rate and the quantitative improvement in amorphous retention are uncertain without alloy-specific thermodynamic and kinetic data.

pool.label: C7
pool.builds_on: The paper emphasizes the impact of quenched disorder on amorphous retention. This hypothesis extends that notion by addressing surface-initiated heterogeneous nucleation, a factor not explored in the paper.
pool.what_is_new: It introduces a surface engineering intervention (passivation coating) to suppress nucleation without altering the bulk composition or the basic cooling/reheating rates, a strategy different from the intrinsic disorder modification discussed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Applying an ultrathin surface passivation coating (e.g. a few nanometers of Al₂O₃) immediately after melt spinning will minimize heterogeneous nucleation at the free surfaces, thereby increasing amorphous retention and thermal stability during subsequent reheating.
fields.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy produced by conventional rapid cooling (melt spinning) that exhibits extensive primary crystallization initiated at free surfaces.
fields.intervention: Deposit an ultrathin (≈2–5 nm) inert Al₂O₃ coating on the as-quenched alloy ribbons using atomic layer deposition (ALD) or a similar technique.
fields.conditions: The alloy should be melt-spun at cooling rates of approximately 10^6–10^7 K s⁻¹ to form ribbons. Immediately after formation, the coating is applied. Reheating in DSC is performed under the same temperature protocols as in the uncoated samples.
fields.structural_mediator: Suppression of heterogeneous nucleation at surfaces.
fields.mechanism: The protective oxide layer reduces surface energy and eliminates surface defects that act as nucleation sites during cooling and reheating. By inhibiting heterogeneous nucleation, the formation of primary crystalline phases is curtailed, facilitating greater retention of the amorphous phase.
fields.predicted_outcome: An increase in the retained amorphous fraction and a higher crystallization onset temperature during moderate reheating, relative to uncoated samples; the improvement is expected to be measurable via a shift in the DSC exothermic peak (potentially on the order of 10–20°C, though the extent remains uncertain).
fields.baseline: Without coating, the alloy shows extensive primary crystallization with a multistep crystallization sequence initiated at the free surfaces during cooling and reheating.
fields.boundary: Rapid cooling rates as used in melt spinning (≥10^6 K s⁻¹) and reheating protocols that typically span the established crystallization temperature range for the uncoated alloy.
fields.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in amorphous retention and thermal stability due to the passivation coating is uncertain and may depend on coating uniformity and thickness.

pool.label: C8
pool.builds_on: The concept that internal stresses and high-energy configurations in amorphous materials can lower thermal stability and prompt crystallization, as discussed in amorphous solid physics.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a specific sub-Tg thermal treatment to kinetically stabilize the amorphous phase, which is not addressed in the paper that focused solely on laser pulse parameters.

fields.hypothesis: Employ a controlled sub-glass-transition (sub-Tg) annealing treatment immediately after rapid quenching to relax residual internal stresses and eliminate high-energy atomic configurations that promote primary crystallization.
fields.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy initially quenched into an amorphous state via rapid cooling, but displaying multistep crystallization upon reheating due to internal stresses and kinetically trapped high-energy sites.
fields.intervention: Introduce a brief thermal hold (anneal) at a temperature slightly below the observed glass transition temperature (Tg - ~20 °C) immediately after rapid solidification, before further cooling or thermal analysis.
fields.conditions: The sub-Tg annealing should be performed for a short duration (on the order of seconds to a minute) and at a temperature below the crystallization onset (e.g., if Tg ~350 °C, annealing at ~330 °C) under an inert atmosphere.
fields.structural_mediator: Relaxation of internal stresses and reorganization of local atomic clusters to a lower energy configuration without triggering crystallization.
fields.mechanism: The annealing near but below Tg allows atoms to undergo minor rearrangements that relieve internal stresses and remove excess free volume. This stabilization minimizes the driving force for primary crystallization during subsequent slower cooling or reheating, thereby enhancing the thermal stability of the amorphous structure.
fields.predicted_outcome: The treated samples would exhibit a higher onset temperature for crystallization in DSC measurements and a reduction in multistep crystallization events, as well as a more pronounced and stable amorphous hump in XRD patterns compared to untreated samples.
fields.baseline: Untreated samples quenched directly from the melt show extensive primary crystallization on reheating, with multiple exothermic peaks in DSC and detectable fcc or oxide phases in XRD.
fields.boundary: The process is effective only when the annealing temperature is sufficiently below the crystallization onset; if the temperature is too close to Tg or maintained for too long, it might inadvertently trigger nucleation.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal time–temperature profile for annealing is uncertain and might vary with minor fluctuations in alloy composition or sample dimension, so only a qualitative improvement is firmly anticipated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of rapidly quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 samples. Immediately anneal one batch at the selected sub-Tg temperature for the prescribed time, while leaving the other batch untreated. Analyze both batches using DSC for crystallization exotherm onset, and XRD for amorphous versus crystalline phase assessment.

XRD patterns for amorphous halo intensity
Microstructural analysis via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant increase in the crystallization onset temperature or an improvement in amorphous phase retention relative to untreated samples, the hypothesis is refuted.

pool.label: C9
pool.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that controlled atomic mobility (via athermal, localized processes) critically dictates crystallization suggests that inhibiting atomic diffusion can stabilize amorphous states. This hypothesis applies that concept by chemically hindering nucleation.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the paper’s findings to a bulk high-entropy alloy system by introducing a minor elemental dopant (boron) to deliberately raise the viscosity and frustration of atomic rearrangements, a route not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Add a minor amount of boron (e.g., 0.5–2 at.%) to the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy to enhance its glass‐forming ability and thermal stability.
fields.material_initial_state: A high-entropy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy that, under conventional rapid and slow cooling as well as subsequent reheating, forms several primary non‐eutectic crystalline phases with a complex crystallization sequence.
fields.intervention: Introduce a trace addition of boron into the melt prior to solidification.
fields.conditions: Test under rapid cooling conditions (cooling rates ~10^6–10^7 K/s, as typical in melt spinning) and slower cooling rates, with reheating up to temperatures close to the crystallization onset (as determined by DSC) to assess retained amorphous fraction.
fields.structural_mediator: Boron atoms tend to increase local packing frustration and act as a kinetic inhibitor to atomic rearrangement by increasing viscosity and disturbing local order.
fields.mechanism: Boron’s small atomic size and its strong affinity for phosphorous and transition metals increase chemical and topological disorder. This interferes with the nucleation and diffusion needed for primary phase formation, thereby shifting the balance toward an amorphous, glassy state even under conditions that would otherwise favor crystallization. The enhanced viscosity retards diffusion during both rapid and moderate cooling, and mitigates crystallization upon reheating.
fields.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase in the retained amorphous fraction (and thermal stability against crystallization) relative to the undoped alloy, with fewer and smaller primary crystalline phases forming. The DSC thermograms should show a delayed exothermic crystallization peak with a potentially broadened glass transition range.
fields.baseline: The undoped Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy which shows extensive primary crystallization under slow cooling and reheating.
fields.boundary: The improvement is expected as long as the boron content remains low enough not to form its own boride crystalline phases, roughly below 2 at.%. At significantly higher boron levels, new crystalline boride phases could emerge, reversing the effect.
fields.uncertainty: While the mechanism of boron-enhanced glass formation is supported in many metallic glass systems, the exact kinetics in this specific high-entropy, phosphorus-containing alloy are not precisely known, so the quantitative improvement in amorphous retention is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy, one with 1 at.% boron and a control without boron. Process both under identical rapid cooling conditions (e.g., melt spinning) and subsequently reheated with a calibrated DSC run. Compare the DSC exotherms and XRD patterns.
measurements: DSC to monitor the onset and intensity of crystallization exotherms
XRD for phase identification and fraction of amorphous vs crystalline content
TEM/SEM to examine microstructural features
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant delay in crystallization onset and a higher amorphous fraction versus the control (or if new boride phases are observed), the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C10
pool.builds_on: The concept that restricting atomic mobility at nucleation sites stabilizes the amorphous phase is derived from the paper’s findings on the importance of atomic level control during phase transitions.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the use of a rare earth dopant, yttrium, as a selective nucleation inhibitor in a high-entropy alloy system, leveraging its size mismatch and segregation behavior—a mechanism and intervention not explored in the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: Doping the alloy with a minor concentration of yttrium (e.g., 0.5–1 at.%) will segregate to potential nucleation sites and inhibit primary crystallization, promoting enhanced amorphous retention and thermal stability.
fields.material_initial_state: The Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy as typically processed shows multiple primary non-eutectic crystalline phases upon cooling with a complex, multistep crystallization sequence.
fields.intervention: Introduce a minor amount of yttrium into the alloy melt.
fields.conditions: Examine the effect under rapid cooling (e.g., melt spinning with cooling rates near 10^6 K/s) and slower cooling regimes; follow with controlled reheating experiments (using DSC) to assess the crystallization kinetics and stability of the amorphous phase.
fields.structural_mediator: Yttrium’s large atomic size leads to local lattice distortions and segregates to grain boundaries or incipient nuclei, thereby raising the nucleation barrier and reducing atomic mobility at critical sites.
fields.mechanism: Yttrium atoms are anticipated to preferentially segregate to regions where crystallization is initiated, increasing interfacial energy and acting as point pinning centers. This segregation not only creates local strain fields that disturb the arrangement required for crystal growth, but also effectively raises the activation energy for crystallite nucleation and growth during both cooling and subsequent reheating.
fields.predicted_outcome: The yttrium-doped alloy should exhibit a marked increase in retained amorphous volume fraction as indicated by a reduced or delayed exothermic crystallization event in DSC and fewer crystalline peaks in XRD. The overall thermal stability upon reheating would improve relative to the undoped alloy.
fields.baseline: The originally reported Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy that shows extensive primary crystallization under the standard processing conditions.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect depends on keeping yttrium concentration low enough to avoid forming separate yttrium-rich intermetallic compounds, typically below about 1 at.%. Excess yttrium might instead act as a new source of heterogeneity leading to other crystallization pathways.
fields.uncertainty: While the segregation behavior of yttrium is well-known in some systems, its exact impact on this multi-element, phosphorus-containing alloy is less certain and may be influenced by complex interactions between elements.

top3.label: C11
top3.builds_on: The finding in the referenced paper that extensive multistep crystallization arises from heterogeneous nucleation events motivates targeting the free volume defects that act as nucleation sites, but here the approach is refined with in-situ free volume characterization tailored to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a material-specific post-quench thermal relaxation treatment—guided by direct free volume quantification—to kinetically inhibit crystallization in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20, rather than employing a generic sub‐Tg annealing used in other metallic glasses.

fields.hypothesis: A tailored sub‐Tg annealing step, calibrated by in-situ free volume measurements, will reduce the specific free volume and defect density in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbons, thus raising the kinetic barrier for primary crystallization and enhancing amorphous retention and thermal stability upon reheating.
fields.material_initial_state: Melt-spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbons produced under standard conditions show extensive multistep crystallization due to a high density of quenched-in free volume and structural defects that act as heterogeneous nucleation sites.
fields.intervention: Immediately after melt spinning, perform a brief, precisely timed annealing treatment at a temperature just below the glass transition (around 600–610 K) for 30–60 seconds in an inert atmosphere. The annealing time and temperature are chosen after preliminary positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) or dilatometry to quantify and target excess free volume unique to this alloy.
fields.conditions: Sub‐Tg isothermal annealing at ~600–610 K for 30–60 seconds followed by thermal analysis (DSC) with reheating at 20 K/min from ~623 K to 1010 K.
fields.structural_mediator: The intervention reduces the free volume and annihilates high-energy defects that otherwise serve as heterogeneous nucleation sites.
fields.mechanism: By decreasing the free volume in the amorphous matrix without crossing Tg into the crystallization regime, the nucleation barrier for primary crystallization is considerably increased. The reduced number of active nucleation sites delays the onset of the multistep crystallization sequence and minimizes the formation of metastable crystalline embryos during subsequent reheating.
fields.predicted_outcome: DSC scans are expected to display an increased crystallization onset temperature and a reduced exothermic enthalpy compared to untreated ribbons. XRD and TEM analyses should reveal a higher fraction of retained amorphous structure with fewer nanoscale crystalline precipitates.
fields.baseline: Untreated melt‐spun Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbons typically exhibit extensive primary crystallization with multiple exothermic events as documented in similar high-entropy glass-forming systems.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect is limited to annealing conditions sufficiently below Tg to avoid any crystallization and requires optimization to account for the alloy’s specific free volume content; excessive time or temperature could instead promote crystallization.
fields.uncertainty: While the expected trend is supported by free volume reduction principles, the exact magnitude of the shift in crystallization temperature and the reduction in crystallinity must be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 ribbons under identical melt-spinning conditions. For one set, immediately perform the sub‐Tg annealing at 600–610 K for 30–60 seconds; keep the other set as-cast. Use PALS to measure free volume differences; then conduct DSC reheating from 623 K to 1010 K (at 20 K/min) and characterize the microstructure by XRD and TEM.
measurements: DSC: Crystallization onset temperature and exothermic enthalpy
PALS or dilatometry: Quantification of free volume
XRD/TEM: Volume fraction and size of crystalline precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in the crystallization onset temperature, a measurable reduction in the exothermic heat release, or a lower crystalline fraction (as measured by XRD/TEM) relative to controls, then the hypothesis is rejected.

top3.label: C10
top3.builds_on: The concept that restricting atomic mobility at nucleation sites stabilizes the amorphous phase is derived from the paper’s findings on the importance of atomic level control during phase transitions.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the use of a rare earth dopant, yttrium, as a selective nucleation inhibitor in a high-entropy alloy system, leveraging its size mismatch and segregation behavior—a mechanism and intervention not explored in the original paper.

fields.hypothesis: Doping the alloy with a minor concentration of yttrium (e.g., 0.5–1 at.%) will segregate to potential nucleation sites and inhibit primary crystallization, promoting enhanced amorphous retention and thermal stability.
fields.material_initial_state: The Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy as typically processed shows multiple primary non-eutectic crystalline phases upon cooling with a complex, multistep crystallization sequence.
fields.intervention: Introduce a minor amount of yttrium into the alloy melt.
fields.conditions: Examine the effect under rapid cooling (e.g., melt spinning with cooling rates near 10^6 K/s) and slower cooling regimes; follow with controlled reheating experiments (using DSC) to assess the crystallization kinetics and stability of the amorphous phase.
fields.structural_mediator: Yttrium’s large atomic size leads to local lattice distortions and segregates to grain boundaries or incipient nuclei, thereby raising the nucleation barrier and reducing atomic mobility at critical sites.
fields.mechanism: Yttrium atoms are anticipated to preferentially segregate to regions where crystallization is initiated, increasing interfacial energy and acting as point pinning centers. This segregation not only creates local strain fields that disturb the arrangement required for crystal growth, but also effectively raises the activation energy for crystallite nucleation and growth during both cooling and subsequent reheating.
fields.predicted_outcome: The yttrium-doped alloy should exhibit a marked increase in retained amorphous volume fraction as indicated by a reduced or delayed exothermic crystallization event in DSC and fewer crystalline peaks in XRD. The overall thermal stability upon reheating would improve relative to the undoped alloy.
fields.baseline: The originally reported Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy that shows extensive primary crystallization under the standard processing conditions.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect depends on keeping yttrium concentration low enough to avoid forming separate yttrium-rich intermetallic compounds, typically below about 1 at.%. Excess yttrium might instead act as a new source of heterogeneity leading to other crystallization pathways.
fields.uncertainty: While the segregation behavior of yttrium is well-known in some systems, its exact impact on this multi-element, phosphorus-containing alloy is less certain and may be influenced by complex interactions between elements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare alloy samples with and without 0.7 at.% yttrium under identical rapid cooling conditions. Use DSC to characterize the onset of crystallization upon reheating and employ XRD/TEM to determine the degree of amorphous retention versus crystalline phase formation.

XRD (to quantify amorphous vs crystalline phase proportions)

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If yttrium-doped samples do not show delayed crystallization onset, reduced crystallinity, or improved thermal stability compared to control samples, or if undesirable yttrium-rich crystalline phases form, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C5
top3.builds_on: The paper’s insight that glass formation is controlled by the competition between icosahedral and crystal-like order under moderate cooling conditions.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies a compositional modification (minor Boron addition) to tailor the atomic-scale structural fluctuations in a complex, multicomponent alloy, an intervention not reported or proposed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: A minor alloying addition of a glass‐forming element (e.g. ~2 at.% Boron) to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 will increase amorphous retention and enhance thermal stability by suppressing the growth of primary crystalline clusters.
fields.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy that undergoes extensive primary crystallization and multistep crystallization during solidification.
fields.intervention: Introduce a small (≈2 at.%) addition of Boron uniformly into the alloy composition.
fields.conditions: The alloy is processed under the same rapid cooling, moderate cooling, and subsequent reheating protocols as before, with cooling rates spanning from below 6.3×10^11 K/s to above 16.6×10^11 K/s, and reheating carried out in the temperature range that shows early crystallization onset (around 750–775 K).
fields.structural_mediator: Enhanced short-range icosahedral order and increased chemical disorder at the atomic level.
fields.mechanism: Boron is known to promote local icosahedral-like ordering and to increase the atomic packing frustration. This extra chemical heterogeneity raises the nucleation barrier for crystalline phases. In this way, the kinetic retardation of atomic rearrangement is enhanced, and the thermodynamic competition between icosahedral and crystal-like order is shifted toward the disordered (amorphous) state. This parallels the paper’s discussion of the competition between icosahedral and crystal-like clusters in the moderate cooling region (PMC4778031::web::009 and PMC4778031::web::014).
fields.predicted_outcome: The boron-doped alloy should exhibit a higher retained amorphous fraction during cooling and a delayed onset of crystallization upon reheating by thermal analysis, compared to the undoped alloy. The improvement is expected to be significant under conditions where the original alloy showed abnormal fluctuations in crystalline fraction.
fields.baseline: The original Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy’s behavior with extensive primary crystallization and fluctuating amorphous fractions in the moderate cooling rate regime.
fields.boundary: Improvement expected when cooling rates are in the critical fluctuation region (approximately 6.3×10^11–16.6×10^11 K/s) and reheating passes through 750–775 K; outside this temperature window, the effect may be less decisive.
fields.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improved thermal stability and the optimum boron content require experimental verification.

Use differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and high-resolution TEM to monitor the onset of crystallization, amorphous fraction, and structural motifs.
